To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
preference reversals between risky choices and bids are accompanied by a shift of fixations from probabilities to amounts.

people systematically exhibit preference reversals when making decisions under risk, and that these preference reversals are accompanied by shifts in visual fixations that reflect changes in the weight given to different attributes of the gamble.
people exhibited systematic changes in attribute fixations and bids when making decisions between two risky gambes, and that these changes were accompanied by systematic preference reversals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying decision making under risk and how they are modulated by context.
the neural mechanisms that support the computation of value during decision under risk.
the role of attention in the construction of value in decision making under risk, and how this process varies with task context.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results presented here provide the first evidence for a link between the visual system, decision making under risk and neural computation of value.

the construction of the value of risky options depends on the task at hand, and that the task directs attention to different attributes of risky gambles, which in turn modulates the computation of value.

the results of the study show that the construction of the value during the decision making under risk is dependent on the task context and that this is partly due to the fact that the task differently directs the attention to the probability or to the amount.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the task context differentially directs attention to different attributes, and that the attention shift is accompanied by changes in neural representations of the attributes.
preference reversals between choice and bidding are accompanied by changes in attention to different attributes, which in turn are reflected in neural signals.
people’s preferences are influenced by the task in which they find themselves.
The main takeaway from our work is that
eye movements provide a window into how task context modulated decision-making.

the same value computation may be used in different tasks and that the task determines the relative weighting of different attributes of the decision problem by modulating the allocation of attention.
preference reversals in decision making under risk are not simply due to changes in the computation of expected value.
